trust_boundaries: developer-to-control-plane: developer kubectl access to k8s_api_server (authenticated via kubeconfig/OIDC)
registry-to-control-plane: image_scanner approval gates image pull via admission webhook
control-plane-to-data-plane: k8s_api_server to kubelet (TLS client cert); scheduler to worker nodes
data-plane-to-storage: container_runtime to secret_store (service account token projection)
observability-to-data-plane: prometheus and log_aggregator scrape/tail from worker nodes
architecture_summary.operational_context: Kubernetes cluster hosting production microservices — public ingress, service mesh, RBAC-controlled API server, etcd with cluster secrets, container registry with image scanning

threat_actors.name: External Web Attacker
threat_actors.motivation: Exploit application vulnerability in a running container to gain a pod foothold and escalate to the cluster
threat_actors.initial_access_vector: Exploit a vulnerability in a workload exposed via ingress controller (e.g. RCE via web framework CVE)
non_capabilities: No initial Kubernetes credentials or service account tokens
No access to control plane network segment without first breaching the data plane
No access to etcd directly — requires control plane pivot

threat_actors.name: Compromised Developer
threat_actors.motivation: Abuse legitimate kubectl access to deploy backdoored workloads or exfiltrate secrets from the cluster
threat_actors.initial_access_vector: Stolen or phished kubeconfig with namespace-scoped permissions
non_capabilities: No cluster-admin role by default — scoped to specific namespaces
No ability to modify admission controller webhook configuration without cluster-admin
No etcd direct read access — API server enforces RBAC on etcd queries

threat_actors.name: Supply Chain Attacker
threat_actors.motivation: Inject a malicious container image into the registry to achieve persistent code execution across all deployments using that image
threat_actors.initial_access_vector: Compromise of a base image in the upstream registry or the CI pipeline that pushes to the internal registry
non_capabilities: No direct Kubernetes API access — relies on image being pulled and run
No ability to bypass image scanner without knowing scanner policy gaps or CVE exemption rules
No network access to cluster internal segments until a pod using the malicious image is running

attack_paths.entry_point: Over-privileged developer kubeconfig or stolen service account token used to deploy a privileged container
attack_paths.impact: Privileged container with host path mount provides node-level access — pivot to all secrets on the node
attack_paths.likelihood_rationale: Privileged container deployment is common in dev-oriented clusters; admission controllers not always enforcing PodSecurity standards

attack_paths.entry_point: Pod service account token with excessive RBAC — list/get Secrets cluster-wide via K8s API
attack_paths.impact: All cluster secrets exposed — database passwords, API keys, TLS certs, registry credentials
attack_paths.likelihood_rationale: Default service accounts in many K8s clusters have broad get/list Secret access; least-privilege RBAC frequently misconfigured

attack_paths.entry_point: CVE in ingress controller (e.g. Nginx annotation injection, Traefik middleware bypass) allows HTTP request manipulation or SSRF
attack_paths.impact: Requests routed to internal services bypassing network policies — access to cluster-internal APIs not intended for public exposure
attack_paths.likelihood_rationale: Ingress controllers have a large CVE surface; annotation injection vulnerabilities have been critical in Nginx ingress controller versions

attack_paths.entry_point: Pod with default automounted service account token uses kubectl within container to enumerate cluster resources
attack_paths.impact: Attacker maps entire cluster topology — namespaces, pods, services, secrets — enabling targeted lateral movement
attack_paths.likelihood_rationale: Kubernetes automounts service account tokens by default; token-based API enumeration is a first step in nearly all K8s intrusions

attack_paths.entry_point: Registry credentials stolen from a CI service account allow pushing a backdoored image over a legitimate tag
attack_paths.impact: Persistent code execution on all pods using the compromised image — persists across pod restarts and redeployments
attack_paths.likelihood_rationale: CI service accounts frequently have registry write access; image tag mutation is not always prevented by immutable tags

attack_paths.entry_point: Container breakout via misconfigured securityContext (privileged: true, hostPID: true, or hostPath mount to /)
attack_paths.impact: Node-level OS access — read all pod secrets from /var/lib/kubelet, access host network, potentially pivot to control plane
attack_paths.likelihood_rationale: Container escape via privileged settings is a well-documented K8s attack; PodSecurity admission not universally enforced

attack_paths.entry_point: Attacker with ClusterRoleBinding create rights creates a new cluster-admin binding for a controlled service account
attack_paths.impact: Persistent cluster-admin access via a new identity — survives kubeconfig rotation and account remediation
attack_paths.likelihood_rationale: Requires existing ClusterRoleBinding write permission (cluster-admin equivalent); high impact but narrower entry requirement

attack_paths.entry_point: Attacker modifies Prometheus scrape config or drops metrics pipelines to suppress anomaly detection alerts
attack_paths.impact: Observability blind spot — resource consumption, lateral movement, and API audit events go undetected
attack_paths.likelihood_rationale: Requires access to Prometheus or cluster RBAC to modify scrape targets; most attackers prioritise exfiltration over detection evasion

mitigations.control_name: PodSecurity admission enforcement — Restricted profile cluster-wide, Baseline minimum in all namespaces
Least-privilege RBAC — no wildcard verbs on Secrets; service account automount disabled by default
Ingress controller version pinned and regularly patched; annotation injection disabled
Disable automountServiceAccountToken on pods and default service accounts; use projected tokens with audience binding
Immutable image tags in registry; admission webhook rejects images not scanned and signed by image_scanner
Prohibit privileged containers and hostPath mounts via admission policy; enforce read-only root filesystem
Audit all ClusterRoleBinding creation; alert on unexpected cluster-admin bindings
Prometheus availability monitoring via external heartbeat; audit log shipping to immutable external SIEM

findings.severity_rationale: Default service account tokens with broad Secret read access are present across multiple namespaces — any pod compromise immediately exposes all cluster credentials without requiring privilege escalation
Privileged containers permitted by absent PodSecurity enforcement — any workload vulnerability becomes a host escape, exposing all other pods on the node
Mutable image tags allow backdoored image to silently replace a legitimate one; image signing not enforced via admission webhook — supply chain risk
Ingress controller CVEs patched promptly via version pinning; residual risk from zero-days; internal service exposure via SSRF is bounded by network policies
Privileged container deployment by developer with over-broad namespace permissions is possible; PodSecurity partial enforcement leaves gaps in lower-trust namespaces
ClusterRoleBinding creation is audited and alerted; RBAC persistence requires prior cluster-admin equivalent, which is a high bar and detectable
Prometheus disruption is detected by external heartbeat within minutes; audit logs ship to external SIEM independently — detection gap is bounded to the heartbeat interval
